client: I've been feeling really off ever since my breakup with Maria about three months ago. Things I used to love, like going hiking with my friends, just don't feel the same anymore — I'll be out on a trail and it's like I'm just going through the motions, not actually enjoying any of it. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: Thank you for giving this a shot — that itself takes courage, especially when you're feeling uncertain it'll help. It sounds like the breakup with Maria has left you feeling a bit disconnected from yourself, like the things that used to bring you joy are now just hollow routines, and I can hear in the way you're speaking that there's a kind of restless unease underneath that — like part of you is still searching for something to hold onto. What we can explore together is how your thoughts during those hikes might be shaping that emptiness, because often it's not that the joy is gone, but that grief is quietly getting in the way of you accessing it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess "disconnected" is a pretty accurate word for it. But I'm not sure I buy the idea that my thoughts are the main thing getting in the way — like, when I'm on the trail, I'm not sitting there consciously thinking about Maria the whole time, it's more like this dull background heaviness that I can't really shake. So I don't know how examining my thoughts is supposed to fix something that feels more like... a weight than a thought.
therapist: That's a really fair pushback, and you're right that grief doesn't always show up as a loud, conscious thought — sometimes it settles in more like a fog, a heaviness that just *is*, and I notice even in the way you're speaking there's something quiet and weighted about it, like you're carrying something you can't quite put down. CBT isn't only about catching obvious thoughts; it's also about noticing the subtle stories we're telling ourselves beneath the surface — things like "nothing feels meaningful anymore" or "I don't know who I am without this relationship" — which can live in the background without us realizing they're shaping everything. Would it feel okay to gently explore whether any of those quieter beliefs might be part of what's making that weight so hard to shake?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that second one kind of lands — "I don't know who I am without this relationship." Maria and I were together for almost four years, and so much of my routine, my weekends, even the way I thought about the future was built around her. But I'm a little worried that if I start pulling at that thread, it's just going to make me feel worse, not better — like, what if I look at all that and there's just... nothing there?
therapist: The fear you're naming — that if you look closely, you might find emptiness — is actually one of the most common and painful fears that comes with a loss like this, and the soft, careful way you're expressing it tells me this touches something really tender and vulnerable for you. But here's a gentle reframe worth considering: the fact that you built so much of your world around this relationship doesn't mean there's *nothing* underneath — it might actually mean you're someone who invests deeply, who values connection and shared futures, and those are qualities that belong to *you*, not to Maria. Pulling at that thread isn't about finding emptiness; it's about slowly rediscovering the person who was there before the relationship, and who's still there now, even if he feels a little unfamiliar right now.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe is... actually kind of hard to argue with, even though part of me wants to. I think what makes it difficult is that I genuinely can't remember who I was before Maria, or at least it feels that blurry — like trying to remember a dream. And I'm not sure "rediscovering" that person sounds comforting so much as it sounds exhausting, like I'd have to do a lot of work just to get back to some baseline I'm not even sure exists anymore.
therapist: The exhaustion in what you're saying feels very real — and I can hear it in your voice too, like even the idea of this process feels like a heavy lift when you're already running low. I want to gently challenge the framing of "getting back to a baseline" though, because this work isn't really about returning to some previous version of yourself — it's more like slowly getting curious about who you are *now*, one small thing at a time, without any pressure to arrive somewhere. That might look less like a big excavation project and more like noticing small moments — even brief ones — where something feels slightly more *you*, and building from there.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Okay, "getting curious" feels a little less daunting than "rediscovering," I'll give you that. But I'm not sure I'd even recognize one of those small moments if it happened — like, on the hike last weekend, there was maybe a second where the view was genuinely nice, but then almost immediately I thought about how Maria would have loved it, and the whole thing just collapsed. I don't know how to stop that from happening, or if I even can.
therapist: What you just described on that hike is actually really important — you *did* notice the view was genuinely nice, even for a second, and that means the capacity for those moments is still there, even if grief is quick to pull you back out of them. The way you're speaking right now — softly, carefully — makes me think this isn't so much about stopping those thoughts about Maria from coming, but learning to let them pass without letting them cancel out what came just before. What if that brief moment of "the view was genuinely nice" and the thought about Maria could both be true at the same time — that you're grieving *and* still capable of beauty landing on you, even now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I've never really thought about it that way — like both things being true at the same time instead of one canceling out the other. But I'm not sure I know how to actually do that in the moment, because when the thought about Maria hits, it doesn't feel like something I can just let pass — it feels like it swallows everything. How do you even train yourself to hold two things at once when one of them feels that heavy?
therapist: The way you're asking that question — softly, carefully, with something that sounds almost like quiet resignation — tells me this doesn't feel like a small or simple thing to you, and it isn't. Learning to hold two feelings at once isn't really a mental trick you force in the moment; it's something that gets built gradually, often starting *after* the wave passes, by gently noticing "that was grief, *and* there was also a beautiful view" — almost like a quiet acknowledgment to yourself once you're back on steadier ground. Over time, that kind of noticing can slowly widen the space between the moment of beauty and the moment grief rushes in, not by making grief lighter, but by making *you* a little more practiced at not letting it have the final word.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That actually makes more sense than I expected — doing the noticing after the fact, not trying to fight the wave while it's happening. But I'm a little skeptical about whether I'd actually remember to do that, because usually by the time I'm back on steadier ground, I just want to not think about the hike at all, you know? Like I kind of just shut the whole experience down and move on, which I'm realizing as I say it out loud is probably not helping me.
therapist: There's something really significant in what you just caught yourself doing — that moment of "I'm realizing as I say it out loud" is exactly the kind of awareness that makes change possible, and I notice there's an energy in your voice right now, like something just clicked or surprised you a little. You're right that shutting the experience down feels protective in the moment, but it also means grief doesn't get processed — it just gets postponed, and the weight stays. What if you gave yourself just one small, low-pressure ritual after a hike — even a single sentence in your phone notes — that acknowledged both things, the hard moment *and* anything that briefly felt okay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: A single sentence in my phone notes feels manageable enough that I can't really argue with it, which is maybe why I'm a little suspicious of it — like, is something that small actually going to do anything? But I think my bigger worry is that writing it down makes it more real, and right now there's something almost comfortable about just letting the hike blur into the background and not having to look at it directly. I guess I'm not sure I'm ready to stop avoiding it, even if I know avoiding it isn't working.
therapist: The honesty in what you just said — "I'm not sure I'm ready to stop avoiding it" — is actually one of the most courageous things you've shared today, and I notice you said it quickly, like it almost slipped out before you could second-guess it. Avoidance makes complete sense as a coping strategy; it *does* protect you from pain in the short term, and there's no pressure to rip that away before you're ready. But what you're already doing right now — looking at the avoidance directly, naming it out loud — is itself a small version of the thing you're afraid to do, and you're handling it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I didn't really think about it that way — that just naming the avoidance out loud is already doing the thing I'm scared of. I think that's actually a little reassuring, even if part of me wonders if I'm just getting credit for something that doesn't count yet. But maybe that's the same voice that shuts down after the hike — the one that decides something doesn't matter before it even gets a chance to.
therapist: The connection you just made — that the voice dismissing your progress might be the same voice that shuts everything down after the hike — is genuinely insightful, and I notice you said it quickly, almost like you were racing to get it out before something stopped you. That voice that decides things "don't count yet" is worth paying attention to, because it's been quietly setting an impossibly high bar for what qualifies as real progress. What if the things that "don't count yet" are actually exactly where change begins?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That idea is sitting with me in a way I didn't expect — like maybe I've been waiting for some big, obvious sign that I'm getting better instead of noticing the smaller things that are actually happening. But I think that voice has been around for a long time, maybe even before Maria, so I'm not sure how much of it is grief and how much is just... me. And if it's just me, I don't know if a single sentence in my phone notes is going to touch something that's been running in the background my whole life.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quickly, with an urgency underneath it — makes me think this realization feels both significant and a little unsettling, like you've stumbled onto something bigger than you expected. You're asking a really important question, and I want to honor it: this voice that dismisses and shuts things down may indeed be older than Maria, but that doesn't make it simply "just you" — it makes it a pattern that learned to protect you somewhere along the way, and patterns like that *can* shift, even long-standing ones. The phone note was never meant to fix everything; it's just one small way of practicing a different voice — one that says "this counts" — and over time, that practice can quietly challenge even the oldest habits.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
